sharedAssociations.basis: Repeated Barbados footprints cover separate snapshot ranges of the same island. The shared geographic account separates the colony, independent monarchy and republic.

scopeNotes: The two imported footprints describe Barbados in separate intervals; their extents were inspected. Sharing an island narrative does not certify their exact geometry or make 1815 a founding date.

Fitzpatrick’s published abstract supports the dated adze and cautions. The full paper was not reviewed. The calibrated range is not equated with the beginning of all human occupation or an identified migration route.

Drewett’s selected field-report passages support the biological and material finds. Older single-shell dates in that report are not repeated as settled chronology. Site-wide food remains are not assigned to one sealed household or ethnic group.
The 1661 law is read as an enslaver-authored prescription. The separate servant code is not confused with the slavery code, and prescribed allowances are not reported as verified provision.
The National Archives teaching resource identifies the colonial provenance of the rebellion documents. Casualty counts and reconstructions of every participant’s intention are omitted.
The emancipation account is a historian’s explanation carried by the Barbados Government Information Service. It distinguishes apprenticeship beginning in 1834 and its ending in 1838.
The official tourism page explains the historical principle of movable chattel houses. Modern retail buildings are not treated as excavated or untouched emancipated households.

Parliament’s historical page supports selected milestones. Its errors about particular early governors, grant funding and the William and Mary institution are not adopted. Disagreement over the precise later reduction of voting age is outside this card.

The government constitution page has an outdated present-tense monarchy description. It is used only for the 1966 historical arrangement; the 2021 transition is separately verified in the official biography’s final paragraph.
Crop Over’s 1974 revival is distinguished from earlier plantation celebrations. No claim of UNESCO intangible-heritage inscription is made.
Poui’s editorial commentary and Green’s own interview are attributed accounts, not claims that every Barbadian shares one language or artistic perspective. No poetry is reproduced.

Source pages with intermittent direct-access errors were checked through indexed text where stated. No historical successor links are invented. Independent review and depth certification remain pending.
